triage.name: Yeast Infections
triage.reason: Common candidal infection with classic vulvovaginal presentation; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and testing.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is one of the most common causes of vaginitis in reproductive-age women
Most women have at least one episode in their lifetime
Uncomplicated episodes occur in otherwise healthy, non-pregnant women
Complicated episodes are more frequent in women with diabetes or immunosuppression

risk_factors.text: Diabetes mellitus, especially poor glycemic control
Use of combined oral contraceptives or high-estrogen contraceptives
Tight, non-breathable clothing and prolonged moisture
Frequent douching or use of scented feminine products

social_history: Sexual activity is not required for vulvovaginal candidiasis, but it can be triggered by intercourse or changes in the vaginal environment
exposures: Prolonged wearing of damp clothing or tight synthetic underwear

chief_complaints.text: It itches down there and it's driving me crazy

hpi.duration: Usually a few days to a week before presentation
hpi.progression: Itching and discharge build up over a few days; symptoms are usually steady rather than coming and going
hpi.quality: Intense itching with a thick, clumpy, white discharge; burning with urination and with intercourse
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; itching is often the most bothersome part
hpi.timing: Constant, often worse at night or after urination

associated_symptoms.text: Thick, white, clumpy discharge (like cottage cheese)
Burning or stinging when urine touches the vulva

pertinent_negatives: Thin gray or green frothy discharge
New or multiple sexual partners with concern for STI

argues_against: Fishy odor and thin gray discharge (bacterial vaginosis)
Frothy green discharge and partner with urethritis (trichomoniasis)
Mucopurulent cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease

negatives: Satellite lesions on thighs or perineum
argues_against: Contact dermatitis or other vulvar dermatoses

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms are often more severe, recurrent and slower to clear; hyperglycemia promotes yeast overgrowth.
More frequent and persistent; treatment is limited to topical azoles for 7 days because oral fluconazole is avoided.
May be severe, recurrent or progress to invasive disease; oral thrush and esophageal involvement are more likely.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis is less common after menopause unless on estrogen therapy or immunosuppressed; consider other causes of vulvar itching and discharge.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; may shift in the chair from itching
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, visibly distracted by itching, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Ill at ease, sore and irritable, avoids sitting still; not toxic-appearing
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with fever and hemodynamic instability — suggests invasive candidiasis rather than uncomplicated vulvovaginal disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva and perineum with good lighting
findings.finding: Diffuse vulvar and labial erythema, sometimes with edema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vaginal vault with a speculum
findings.finding: Thick, white, clumpy discharge adherent to the vaginal walls

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vaginal mucosa during speculum exam
findings.finding: Erythematous vaginal mucosa with white plaques or patches

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulvar skin for scratch marks
Perform bimanual exam with cervical motion
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness and no adnexal mass or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Assess vaginal discharge odor (whiff test if discharge present)
Inspect the cervix for mucopurulent discharge or friability
findings.finding: No mucopurulent cervical discharge or easily induced bleeding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva, vagina and perineum for ulcers or vesicles
findings.finding: No ulcers, vesicles or inguinal lymphadenopathy

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen, including suprapubic and lower quadrants
Inspect the oral mucosa, tongue and pharynx
findings.finding: White plaques that scrape off leaving an erythematous base (thrush)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk, extremities and intertriginous areas
findings.finding: No satellite lesions or rash outside the vulvar area

labs.caveat: Negative. Ordered in anyone of reproductive age with vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain or missed period before attributing symptoms to candidiasis; rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy.
May be elevated in undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes, which predisposes to recurrent or complicated vulvovaginal candidiasis.
Screens for diabetes in recurrent or complicated episodes; not needed for a first uncomplicated episode.
Usually normal in uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis. Marked leukocytosis or leukopenia suggests invasive candidiasis or another systemic process.
Only relevant when invasive candidiasis or candidemia is suspected; azole dosing and nephrotoxic risk are affected by renal function.

findings.text: Budding yeast, pseudohyphae or hyphae seen on saline or 10% KOH preparation
Normal-appearing squamous epithelial cells without clue cells
Growth of Candida species, most often C. albicans
Growth of a non-albicans species such as C. glabrata (more likely in recurrent or azole-refractory cases)
Multiple pulmonary nodules or cavitary lesions in invasive candidiasis
No nodules or consolidation in uncomplicated localized disease
Hepatosplenic microabscesses (echogenic foci) in chronic disseminated candidiasis

initial.why: First-line bedside test; shows budding yeast, pseudohyphae or hyphae and excludes bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis
Normal pH (4.0–4.5) supports candidiasis and argues against bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before treatment or imaging
initial.only_if: reproductive-age patient with missed period, pelvic pain or abnormal bleeding

initial.why: Looks for undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes in recurrent or complicated episodes
initial.only_if: recurrent, severe or complicated vulvovaginal candidiasis

confirmatory.why: Confirms Candida and identifies the species when microscopy is negative but suspicion remains high, or when symptoms are recurrent or refractory to azoles

supporting.why: Screens for diabetes as a driver of recurrent infection
Assesses for systemic infection when invasive candidiasis is suspected
Baseline renal function before systemic antifungal therapy
supporting.only_if: systemic antifungal treatment is planned or invasive disease is suspected

supporting.why: Evaluates for pulmonary involvement in suspected invasive candidiasis
supporting.only_if: persistent fever, respiratory symptoms or immunocompromise with suspected invasive disease

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis
Not routinely needed unless systemic illness or antifungal therapy requires monitoring
External dysuria is from vulvar irritation, not a urinary tract infection; testing may mislead
Nonspecific and not useful in localized vulvovaginal disease
Only for suspected hepatosplenic candidiasis in immunocompromised patients
not_indicated.only_if: immunocompromised with suspected chronic disseminated candidiasis

decision_points: Confirm the diagnosis with wet mount or culture before starting antifungal therapy when the presentation is atypical or recurrent
Check vaginal pH: normal pH supports candidiasis; elevated pH suggests bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis
Pregnancy test before systemic azole therapy in anyone who could be pregnant
Consider diabetes screening in recurrent or complicated cases
Escalate to imaging and blood cultures when fever, hemodynamic instability or immunocompromise suggests invasive candidiasis

differential.name: Bacterial vaginosis
differential.why_considered: Vaginal discharge and vulvar irritation are the most common reasons women present with vaginitis, and bacterial vaginosis is the most frequent cause of abnormal discharge.

history: Thin, gray-white discharge with a fishy odor, often worse after intercourse or menses
exam: Thin, homogeneous gray discharge coating the vaginal walls
Positive whiff test (fishy amine odor with KOH)
No significant vulvar erythema or edema
labs: Clue cells on saline wet mount
Absence of budding yeast or pseudohyphae

differential.name: Trichomoniasis
differential.why_considered: Causes vaginal discharge, itching and dysuria, overlapping with candidal vaginitis.

history: Symptoms often worse during or after menses
exam: Vulvar and vaginal erythema with petechial spots (strawberry cervix)
May have cervical motion tenderness if concurrent pelvic inflammatory disease
labs: Motile trichomonads on saline wet mount
Positive nucleic acid amplification test for Trichomonas vaginalis

differential.name: Chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis
differential.why_considered: Mucopurulent discharge, dysuria and pelvic discomfort can be mistaken for a yeast infection, and untreated infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility.
differential.trigger: Mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, or a new sexual partner with concern for sexually transmitted infection

history: Mucopurulent discharge rather than clumpy white discharge
exam: Cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Elevated white blood cell count in some cases

differential.name: Contact dermatitis or vulvar dermatosis
differential.why_considered: Vulvar itching, burning and erythema can mimic candidiasis, especially with exposure to soaps, detergents, or scented products.

history: Exposure to new soap, detergent, fabric softener, or feminine hygiene product
Symptoms improve with avoidance of the irritant
exam: Erythema and excoriation limited to areas of contact

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Dysuria is a common symptom of both candidal vulvitis and urinary tract infection.

history: Internal dysuria with urgency and frequency
exam: No costovertebral angle tenderness in uncomplicated cystitis
labs: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis

differential.name: Genital herpes simplex virus infection
differential.why_considered: Vulvar pain, burning and dysuria can resemble candidal vulvitis, particularly during a primary outbreak.

history: Prodrome of tingling or burning before lesions appear
exam: Grouped vesicles or shallow ulcers on erythematous base
labs: Positive herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction from a lesion swab

severity.mild: Mild itching and scant discharge; minimal vulvar erythema; no fissures or excoriation; patient comfortable and not distressed
severity.moderate: Moderate itching and burning; noticeable thick white discharge; vulvar erythema and edema; dysuria and dyspareunia; patient distracted by symptoms but otherwise well
severity.severe: Intense itching and soreness; marked vulvar erythema, edema, fissures or excoriation; patient irritable and avoids sitting; may have low-grade fever; consider complicated or recurrent disease
severity.critical: Not applicable to uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis; high fever, hypotension or toxic appearance should prompt evaluation for invasive candidiasis or another systemic infection

red_flags.meaning: Suggests invasive candidiasis or another systemic infection rather than uncomplicated vulvovaginal disease

red_flags.finding: Pelvic or lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, or adnexal tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another upper genital tract infection
Suggests bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis rather than candidiasis

red_flags.finding: Mucopurulent cervical discharge or cervical friability
Vaginal bleeding or missed period in a reproductive-age patient
red_flags.meaning: Requires pregnancy testing to rule out ectopic pregnancy or other causes

red_flags.finding: Immunocompromise with oral thrush, odynophagia, or persistent fever
red_flags.meaning: Suggests esophageal or invasive candidiasis requiring systemic therapy and further workup

complications.name: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
clues: Four or more symptomatic episodes in 12 months
Often associated with diabetes or immunosuppression

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection of excoriated skin
clues: Increasing pain, warmth, or purulent drainage from vulvar skin

complications.name: Esophageal candidiasis
clues: Immunocompromise such as HIV or transplant

special_populations.differences: More frequent and persistent; treatment is limited to topical azoles for 7 days because oral fluconazole is avoided. Recurrence is common.
Symptoms are often more severe, recurrent and slower to clear; hyperglycemia promotes yeast overgrowth. Glycemic control is part of management.
May be severe, recurrent or progress to invasive disease; oral thrush and esophageal involvement are more likely. Systemic antifungal therapy may be needed.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis is less common after menopause unless on estrogen therapy or immunosuppressed; consider other causes of vulvar itching and discharge.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis can occur in prepubertal girls, often associated with antibiotic use, diabetes, or poor hygiene; consider sexual abuse if there are other concerning findings.

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like — color, thickness, and smell?
key_questions.looking_for: Thick, white, clumpy discharge without a foul or fishy odor

key_questions.question: How bad is the itching, and when did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Intense vulvar itching building over 1–3 days, often the most bothersome symptom

key_questions.question: Does it burn when urine passes over the vulva, or does the burning feel inside?
key_questions.looking_for: External dysuria from urine touching irritated vulvar skin rather than internal urinary burning

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics recently, or used steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics or corticosteroids — classic triggers for candidal overgrowth

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, HIV, or any condition or medication that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or immunosuppression, which makes episodes more severe, recurrent, or complicated

key_questions.question: Have you had yeast infections before? How many in the past year?
key_questions.looking_for: Four or more episodes in 12 months suggests recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or pain in your lower belly or pelvis?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in uncomplicated disease; present suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or invasive infection

key_questions.question: Any abnormal vaginal bleeding, spotting, or a missed period?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; bleeding or a missed period requires pregnancy testing to exclude ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes treatment — topical azoles for 7 days instead of oral fluconazole

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any sores, blisters, or ulcers on the genitals?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; painful vesicles or ulcers suggest genital herpes

key_questions.question: Do you have a new sexual partner, or any concern about a sexually transmitted infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis and trichomoniasis

key_questions.question: Have you used any new soaps, detergents, or feminine hygiene products?
key_questions.looking_for: Irritant exposure suggesting contact dermatitis rather than infection

key_questions.question: Have you tried any over-the-counter yeast treatment, and did it help?
key_questions.looking_for: Partial or no response raises concern for a non-albicans species or the wrong diagnosis

reasoning_points: Intense vulvar itching with a thick, white, clumpy discharge and no foul odor
Recent antibiotic use, diabetes, pregnancy, or immunosuppression as a predisposing factor
Vulvar and vaginal erythema with thick white discharge on speculum exam and no cervical motion tenderness
Normal vaginal pH (4.0–4.5) with budding yeast, pseudohyphae, or hyphae on wet mount
No clue cells, no motile trichomonads, and a negative whiff test
Pregnancy excluded before systemic azole therapy in a reproductive-age patient
Red flags such as fever, pelvic pain, or mucopurulent cervical discharge are absent

easy: Reproductive-age woman with classic intense itching and cottage-cheese discharge
Recent course of antibiotics as a clear trigger
Vulvar erythema with thick white discharge on exam
Wet mount showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae
medium: External dysuria mistaken for a urinary tract infection
Recurrent episodes in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes
Pregnant patient who cannot receive oral fluconazole
Mixed discharge picture requiring wet mount and pH to separate from bacterial vaginosis
hard: Non-albicans species such as C. glabrata with negative microscopy and azole-refractory symptoms
Postmenopausal woman on estrogen therapy with vulvar itching and scant discharge
Immunocompromised patient with oral thrush and odynophagia suggesting esophageal candidiasis
Persistent fever despite antibiotics in a patient with a central line suggesting candidemia
